people.name: María Hoyos
body: On East Franklin Avenue in the Phillips neighborhood of Minneapolis, Maria's Café is known for its cachapas: large corn pancakes, listed on the menu as Cachapas Venezolanas, with bits of fresh corn in the batter and crisp edges. Heavy Table described them in a 2014 review. The woman behind the café, María Hoyos, did not set out to become a breakfast cook.

Hoyos came to Minneapolis from Medellín, Colombia. Explore Minnesota and the café's own website date her arrival to 1980, and the neighborhood paper the alley dates it to 1979. She owned a florist shop, and by her account cooking was a hobby that "evolved into a calling." She spent about 14 years at a popular South Minneapolis restaurant, then opened her own place, Maria's Breakfast Club, in 1993. Business grew quickly. When the lease ended, she moved the restaurant, but the move did not work out. For a time she did private catering and cooked at country clubs.

Her comeback came with an invitation from an American Indian development corporation to open in the Ancient Traders Market at 1113 East Franklin Avenue. Maria's Café opened there in 1999, according to the alley. In January 2010, Mayor R.T. Rybak and the Minneapolis City Council gave the café a Business Resolution award for ten years at that location. She told the alley, "I really enjoy helping those in need."
As of October 2026, the café's website lists her as owner and operator and shows the menu, weekend specials, and weekend live music.
keyFacts: Came to Minneapolis from Medellín, Colombia, in 1979 or 1980 (sources differ).
1993: Opened Maria's Breakfast Club.
1999: Opened Maria's Café at 1113 East Franklin Avenue.
2010: Business Resolution award from the mayor and City Council.
people.connectToWork: When a neighborhood business is the place people already go, how would you find out whether it wants any part in your outreach, and what would you offer in return?

people.name: Martha Ordóñez Daniels
body: On December 9, 2023, Colombia Live staged La Cucharita at The Wellstone Center in St. Paul. The sold-out, two-hour production combined 17 dances, six short sketches, 36 dancers and 180 costumes, drawing on dances from many regions of Colombia. Its executive director is Martha Ordóñez Daniels.

According to MPR News, Ordóñez Daniels was born in Colombia and started dancing in school performances. She joined a folklore group in Atlanta and stopped when she moved to the Twin Cities. A few years later she saw the Latin dance group Fuego Latino and joined it. GiveMN dates her joining to 2004. She enrolled her daughter too.

The group became Grupo de Danzas Colombianas in 2007 under her leadership. In September 2023 it became a nonprofit and took the name Colombia Live, because the old name was hard for English speakers to pronounce or write. It teaches four age groups, from preschoolers to adults. It has performed at the Festival of Nations, the Minneapolis Aquatennial and Valleyfair, and MPR News reported that it was the first dance group to represent Colombia at the Minnesota State Fair.

MPR News reported that its younger dancers are mostly second-generation Colombian, and that adoptive families of children from Colombia find the group and enroll their kids. One family told MPR the group is like a second family. As of October 2026, its GiveMN page shows a campaign for 2026 workshops with guest teachers from Colombia.
keyFacts: Born in Colombia; joined Fuego Latino in the Twin Cities in 2004, per GiveMN.
2007: Group became Grupo de Danzas Colombianas under her leadership.
September 2023: Became the nonprofit Colombia Live.
December 9, 2023: La Cucharita at The Wellstone Center, St. Paul.
people.connectToWork: If someone you work with grew up away from the culture of their birth family, how would you ask what connection they want, without assuming they want one or that they already have it?

people.name: Luis Patiño
body: On January 1, 2011, a Minneapolis paralegal made a New Year's resolution to stop thinking about a food business and start one. Luis Patiño sold two motorcycles, saved a 20 percent down payment on a $45,000 loan, and went to seven or eight banks over about eight months before he got financing. His food truck, Cafe Racer, took its name from motorcycle culture. Its menu came from the home cooking of his mother and grandmother. "This food is directly influenced by the peasant-style food I grew up eating," he told Heavy Table in 2013.

Patiño was born in Colombia and came to the United States as a child. He graduated from Hamline University in St. Paul and worked as a paralegal. His wife, Christine, is his business partner. In the truck's first full season, his crew prepped overnight in borrowed kitchen space at Tiger Sushi on Lyndale Avenue.

Mpls.St.Paul Magazine called the truck one of the first to serve the Colombian street dog, a hot dog with toppings such as pico verde and queso fresco. In spring 2015 he opened a restaurant, Cafe Racer Kitchen, at 2929 East 25th Street in Minneapolis, near the border of the Seward and Longfellow neighborhoods. As of October 2026, its website lists that address, with hours, and describes a restaurant and catering company.
keyFacts: Born in Colombia; came to the U.S. as a child.
Graduated from Hamline University; worked as a paralegal.
January 1, 2011: Committed to starting the Cafe Racer truck.
Spring 2015: Opened Cafe Racer Kitchen in Minneapolis.
people.connectToWork: Does a program you work on assume people can get a loan, a license or a lease on the first try? What happens to someone who needs eight months and seven banks?

people.name: Anika Fajardo
body: At 21, Anika Fajardo traveled to Colombia to meet the father she had not seen since she was a baby. Her own account describes swimming in the natural hot springs at Coconuco, in the Andes, while she tried to work out who this man was and what being Colombian meant for her. She later turned that trip, and the questions before it, into a memoir she worked on for about nine years.
Fajardo was born in Colombia and raised in Minnesota, and she lives in Minneapolis. Her parents divorced, and she grew up in Minnesota away from her Colombian relatives.

Her memoir, Magical Realism for Non-Believers: A Memoir of Finding Family, was published by the University of Minnesota Press in 2019. The manuscript was a finalist for the Bakeless Literary Prize in Creative Nonfiction, and the book was a finalist for the 2020 Minnesota Book Award.

She has since written for younger readers and adults. Her site lists What If a Fish, which won a 2021 Minnesota Book Award, Meet Me Halfway, Waiting on a Miracle, and the novel The Many Mothers of Dolores Moore, which won a 2025 International Latino Book Award gold medal. She has had support from the Jerome Foundation, the Minnesota State Arts Board and the Loft Literary Center. As of October 2026, her site says she teaches in Augsburg University's MFA program and founded the author group MN BIPOC Kidlit Creators.
keyFacts: Born in Colombia; raised in Minnesota; lives in Minneapolis.
2019: Published Magical Realism for Non-Believers.
2020: Minnesota Book Award finalist for the memoir.
2021: Minnesota Book Award for What If a Fish.
2025: International Latino Book Award gold medal for The Many Mothers of Dolores Moore.
people.connectToWork: A form may ask for one country, one language or one family. Whose life does your form leave no room for, and how would you find out?

people.name: John Leguizamo
body: In 2017, struck by how few Latinos appeared in his son's American history class, John Leguizamo wrote a one-man show to fill the gap. Latin History for Morons ran at The Public Theater from February to April 2017 and moved to Broadway's Studio 54 that fall, opening officially on November 15. It earned a Tony nomination for Best Play, and Leguizamo received a Special Tony Award in 2018 for his body of work and for bringing diverse stories and audiences to Broadway over three decades.

Leguizamo was born in Bogotá on July 22, 1964, according to Biography.com and New York Theatre Guide. His family moved to Queens when he was about four. He left New York University to do stand-up. His breakthrough was a series of solo shows in which he played many characters from Latino New York: Mambo Mouth, which won an Obie Award and an Outer Critics Circle Award, and Spic-O-Rama, which won Lucille Lortel and Theatre World awards. Freak went to Broadway in 1998 and earned two Tony nominations and a Drama Desk Award, and its 1999 HBO version won him an Emmy. Ghetto Klown (2011) won a second Drama Desk Award.

On screen he appeared in Carlito's Way, Romeo + Juliet and Moulin Rouge!, was nominated at the Golden Globes for To Wong Foo, Thanks for Everything! Julie Newmar, and voiced Sid the Sloth in the Ice Age films.
keyFacts: Born in Bogotá; moved to Queens as a young child.
Mambo Mouth (Off-Broadway, 1990–91): Obie Award.
1999: Emmy Award for HBO's Freak.
2017: Latin History for Morons at The Public Theater, then Broadway.
2018: Special Tony Award.
people.connectToWork: Whose history is missing from the materials your program hands out or teaches from, and who would you ask about it?

people.name: Diane Guerrero
body: Diane Guerrero was 14 when she came home from school in Boston to find her parents gone. Immigration authorities had detained them in spring 2001, and they were deported to Colombia. She was a U.S. citizen, born in New Jersey on July 21, 1986. Publishers Weekly's review of her memoir says she was left "with no government oversight whatsoever." Friends and family took her in and helped her enroll at the Boston Arts Academy.

Kirkus Reviews reports that her parents entered in 1991 on a 90-day visitor visa and stayed past its end. Publishers Weekly adds that they tried to gain legal status and were defrauded by a con artist. In the memoir she describes the depression that followed, and the help she found when she confided in a therapist.

She became known for her roles on Orange Is the New Black and Jane the Virgin. In November 2014 she told her family's story in a Los Angeles Times op-ed. In 2016 she published In the Country We Love: My Family Divided, written with Michelle Burford, which won a 2017 Alex Award from the American Library Association. Publishers Weekly notes her work as a White House Ambassador for Citizenship and Naturalization, and Kirkus her volunteering for the Immigrant Legal Resource Center.
keyFacts: July 21, 1986: Born in New Jersey to Colombian parents.
2001: Parents detained and deported when she was 14.
November 2014: Los Angeles Times op-ed.
2016: Published In the Country We Love: My Family Divided.
2017: Alex Award for the memoir.
people.connectToWork: If a child you serve loses a parent to detention or deportation, who in your system would know, whose job is it to check on the child, and what information would the family need to trust you with?

people.name: Rodolfo Llinás
body: For decades, Rodolfo Llinás has recorded electrical signals from single nerve cells to understand how the brain works. His research runs from the giant synapse of the squid to human brain scans using magnetoencephalography, and it covers the cerebellum, thalamus and cortex. He introduced the idea of "thalamocortical dysrhythmia," which links disrupted rhythms between the thalamus and cortex to several neurological and psychiatric conditions.

Llinás was born in Bogotá on December 16, 1934. He attended the Gimnasio Moderno school, earned his medical degree at Universidad Javeriana in Bogotá, and earned a PhD at the Australian National University, working under Nobel laureate Sir John Eccles. From 1976 he chaired the Department of Physiology and Neuroscience at New York University School of Medicine, where he held the Thomas and Suzanne Murphy professorship.

He chaired NASA's Neurolab Science Working Group and wrote I of the Vortex: From Neurons to Self. He is a member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the American Philosophical Society, and academies in Spain and France. In Colombia, he was one of the ten commissioners of the Misión de Sabios, which delivered its report on education and development to President César Gaviria on July 21, 1994. In a 2014 Semana article he criticized how little of it had been carried out.
keyFacts: December 16, 1934: Born in Bogotá.
MD, Universidad Javeriana; PhD, Australian National University.
1976: Became chair of Physiology and Neuroscience, NYU School of Medicine.
Member, U.S. National Academy of Sciences.
1994: Commissioner of Colombia's Misión de Sabios.
people.connectToWork: When you meet someone who moved from another country, how do you avoid guessing at their education or profession, and where in your process would you actually ask?

people.name: Jaime Manrique
body: Jaime Manrique was 17 when he moved from Colombia to Florida with his mother and sister. He has spent his career working in two languages. He was born in Barranquilla, on Colombia's Caribbean coast, on June 16, 1949, and earned a BA from the University of South Florida in 1972. His first poetry collection, Los adoradores de la luna, won Colombia's Eduardo Cote Lamus National Poetry Award in 1975.

His novels include Latin Moon in Manhattan, Twilight at the Equator, Our Lives Are the Rivers, which won a 2007 International Latino Book Award, and Cervantes Street (2012). In the essay collection Eminent Maricones: Arenas, Lorca, Puig, and Me (2002), he writes about gay Latin American writers and his own life. With Joan Larkin he translated the love poems of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz.

He received a Guggenheim Fellowship and a New York Foundation for the Arts fellowship, both in 2000. He was a visiting professor at Mount Holyoke and taught in Columbia University's MFA program. The Academy of American Poets lists him as teaching at the City College of New York and living in New York City.
keyFacts: 1949: Born in Barranquilla, Colombia.
Moved to Florida at 17.

people.name: Juan C. Zapata
body: In 2002, voters in a Miami-Dade County district sent Juan Carlos Zapata to Tallahassee. His legislative profile lists him as the first Colombian American elected to the Florida Legislature.

That profile says he was born in Medellín, Colombia, on December 9, 1966, and moved to Florida in 1977. Miami Today, in a 2013 profile, says he was born in Peru to Colombian parents. Both agree on his family's Colombian roots and on 1977. He earned an associate degree at Miami-Dade Community College and a bachelor's degree from Florida International University in 1994. Before running for state office he chaired the West Kendall Community Council and served on Miami-Dade County's Equal Opportunity Board and Planning Advisory Board.

A Republican, he represented House District 119 from 2002 until term limits ended his service in 2010. He chaired the Miami-Dade Legislative Delegation and the Board of Hispanic Caucus Chairs. Nationally, he chaired the NALEO Educational Fund, the nonprofit arm of the National Association of Latino Elected and Appointed Officials, and a National Conference of State Legislatures committee. He then won a seat on the Miami-Dade County Commission, District 11, in 2012, and was still in that seat in May 2016. He no longer holds the seat; as of October 2026 the county lists Roberto J. Gonzalez as the District 11 commissioner.
keyFacts: Moved to Florida in 1977.
1994: B.S., Florida International University.
2002–2010: Florida House of Representatives, District 119.
Elected 2012: Miami-Dade County Commissioner, District 11; in the seat through at least May 2016.
people.connectToWork: When you plan outreach, whose political views or party do you assume from a name or a language, and what would change if you did not?

people.name: Patricia Engel
body: In 2017, Patricia Engel won the fiction prize of the Dayton Literary Peace Prize for The Veins of the Ocean (2016), a novel about Reina Castillo, a Colombian American woman whose life is shaped by her brother's imprisonment, as she looks for her own kind of freedom.
Engel was born to Colombian parents and raised in New Jersey. She lives in Miami, where the Dayton prize lists her as teaching creative writing at the University of Miami.

Her first book, Vida (2010), is a linked collection of stories about a young Colombian American woman. It was a New York Times Notable Book of the Year and a finalist for the PEN/Hemingway Award. Her site says it won Colombia's Premio Biblioteca de Narrativa Colombiana in 2017, and that she was the first woman to win that prize. Her novel It's Not Love, It's Just Paris won an International Latino Book Award. In 2014 she received a National Endowment for the Arts literature fellowship, and her stories appeared in The Best American Short Stories 2017.
Infinite Country, a New York Times bestseller, tells of a Colombian family divided between Bogotá and the United States by immigration status. Her collection The Faraway World was published in 2023.
keyFacts: Born to Colombian parents; raised in New Jersey; lives in Miami.
2010: Vida.
2014: National Endowment for the Arts fellowship.
2017: Dayton Literary Peace Prize for fiction.

people.name: Edgar Rentería
body: In the bottom of the 11th inning of Game Seven of the 1997 World Series, with the bases loaded, young shortstop Edgar Rentería lined a single that won the Florida Marlins the championship. Thirteen years later, playing for the San Francisco Giants, he hit a go-ahead home run in Game Five and was named Most Valuable Player of the 2010 World Series.

Rentería grew up in Barranquilla, on Colombia's Caribbean coast, the youngest of seven children. His father died when he was one, and the family got by selling candy, pork rinds and raffle tickets. His older brother Edinson taught him baseball. The Marlins signed him at 15. His SABR biography notes that Major League Baseball lists his birth year as 1975, while his brother said the family altered the birth certificate so he could sign young. Baseball-Reference gives August 7, 1976.

He played in the major leagues from 1996 through 2011 for seven teams, was a five-time All-Star, and won two Gold Gloves and three Silver Sluggers. After the 1997 title, by SABR's account, Colombia's president gave him the country's highest honor. SABR also credits him with inspiring Colombian children to take up baseball. In March 2018 the Edgar Rentería National Baseball Stadium opened in Barranquilla.
keyFacts: Born in Barranquilla (1975 per MLB; August 7, 1976 per Baseball-Reference).
Signed by the Florida Marlins at 15; major league debut 1996.
1997: Winning hit in Game Seven of the World Series.
2010: World Series MVP with San Francisco.
2018: Edgar Rentería National Baseball Stadium opened in Barranquilla.
people.connectToWork: When a person's documents and their family's account differ on something like a birth date, what does your process do, and who bears the cost of sorting it out?

people.name: Nina García
body: In September 2017, Hearst named Nina García editor-in-chief of Elle. Bravo describes her as the "first Latina to lead a major American fashion title." Television viewers already knew her as a judge on Project Runway, where she has sat on the panel since the show launched in 2004.

García was born in Barranquilla, Colombia, in 1965, and came to the United States at 15, according to the Fashion Institute of Technology's alumni magazine. She attended a girls' high school in Wellesley, Massachusetts, then studied at Boston University, at ESMOD in Paris, and at FIT in New York. She began her career at Mirabella and joined Elle in 1995, serving as fashion director from 2000 to 2008. She then moved to Marie Claire, where she was creative director from 2012, before returning to lead Elle.

Bravo says she has written four New York Times bestselling style books and has worked as a style expert on Today, Good Morning America and The View. A 2026 Fashion Trust Arabia profile lists her as Elle's editor-in-chief.

people.name: Kali Uchis
body: At the 2021 Grammy Awards, the song "10%," by producer Kaytranada and singer Kali Uchis, won Best Dance/Electronic Recording. The same year her Spanish-language song "Telepatía" reached No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Latin Songs chart and became her first solo hit on the Hot 100, where it stayed for 23 weeks.

Uchis was born Karly Marina Loaiza on July 17, 1994, in Alexandria, Virginia, to a Colombian father and an American mother, the youngest of five children. She has described early years in Pereira, in Colombia, and grew up moving between Pereira and Virginia. She records in both English and Spanish.

Her debut album, Isolation, came out in 2018. Sin Miedo (del Amor y Otros Demonios) (2020), largely in Spanish, reached No. 1 on Billboard's Top Latin Albums chart. Red Moon in Venus (2023) reached No. 4 on the Billboard 200, and Orquídeas (2024) and Sincerely (2025) each debuted at No. 2. Orquídeas was also nominated for a Latin Grammy for Best Pop Vocal Album.

people.name: Catalina Cruz
body: When Catalina Cruz took office in the New York State Assembly in 2019, she represented the Queens neighborhoods where she had arrived from Colombia at age nine: Corona, Elmhurst and Jackson Heights. She won the seat in November 2018, at 35. NY1 reported that she was the first Dreamer and the first Colombian-born politician elected to the Assembly.

Her official biography says she lived in the United States for more than ten years as an undocumented American. "Dreamers" is the common term for people brought to the U.S. as children without legal status, named for the long-debated DREAM Act.

She earned a bachelor's degree at John Jay College of Criminal Justice and a law degree at the CUNY School of Law. She practiced housing law, then served as chief of staff to New York City Council Member Julissa Ferreras-Copeland and as counsel to the City Council's Committee on Immigration. She later directed the Governor's Exploited Workers Task Force.
As of October 2026, she represents Assembly District 39, and her biography says she has passed more than 20 laws since taking office. Assembly seats are on the ballot on November 3, 2026.

people.name: Aileen Cannon
body: On November 12, 2020, the U.S. Senate confirmed Aileen Mercedes Cannon as a judge of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida. She was nominated by President Donald J. Trump on May 21, 2020, and received her commission on November 13. As of October 2026, the court lists her as a district judge, with chambers in the federal courthouse in Fort Pierce.

Cannon was born in 1981 in Cali, Colombia. News profiles citing The New York Times and the Miami Herald report that her mother left Cuba as a girl after the 1959 revolution and that her father's family is from Indiana. She grew up in Miami. She earned a B.A. from Duke University in 2003 and a J.D. magna cum laude from the University of Michigan Law School in 2007.

After law school she clerked for federal appeals judge Steven M. Colloton from 2008 to 2009, practiced law in Washington, D.C., from 2009 to 2012, and served as an assistant U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Florida from 2013 to 2020.

people.name: Mariana Lozano
body: In December 2023, Human Rights Watch named Mariana Lozano, a young Colombian activist, the fourth recipient of its Marca Bristo Fellowship for Leadership in Disability Rights. Lozano describes herself as a woman with an intellectual disability. Human Rights Watch wrote that she has overcome stigma and exclusion and built life skills such as financial literacy and personal safety.

She is part of Coopmente, a cooperative that supports people with intellectual disabilities and their families. As a university student she is also studying the legal protections for people with intellectual disabilities. "I want people with intellectual disabilities to be visible," she told Human Rights Watch.

On June 13, 2024, as a Marca Bristo Fellow, she spoke on a panel at the 17th Conference of States Parties to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, on decent work and sustainable livelihoods. She lives in Colombia and is not Colombian American. Her story is here because she speaks for herself about making her own decisions.
keyFacts: Colombian self-advocate with an intellectual disability.
Part of Coopmente.
2023: Human Rights Watch Marca Bristo Fellow.

people.name: Juan Pablo Salazar
body: Juan Pablo Salazar is from Bogotá. La Silla Vacía, writing in February 2015, reported that he had become paraplegic after an accident about ten years earlier, that he founded the Arcángeles Foundation, a rehabilitation center that helps people with disabilities find work, and that he was the creative mind behind the "Remángate" campaign about landmine victims. It also reported that he had led the Colombian Paralympic Committee for about two years.

The Inter-American Dialogue lists him as a former president of Colombia's National Council on Disability and a former director of the Presidential Plan for the Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities. A 2021 conference biography named him as a Governing Board member of the International Paralympic Committee. The Dialogue's profile lists him as inclusion coordinator at CAF, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and as vice president of the Organization of American States committee working to end discrimination against people with disabilities.
He lives in Colombia and is not Colombian American. Someone arriving from Colombia may know his work.
keyFacts: From Bogotá; marketing degree from Universidad Jorge Tadeo Lozano.
Founded Fundación Arcángeles.
Led the Colombian Paralympic Committee and the National Council on Disability.
Inclusion coordinator at CAF, per the Inter-American Dialogue.
people.connectToWork: When you talk about disability with someone new to your service, whose leadership and which public campaigns might they already know that you do not? How would you find out?

institutions.name: Centro Cívico Colombiano
body: In June 2010, Rep. Joseph Crowley toured a new computer lab at the Centro Cívico Colombiano in Elmhurst, bought with $50,000 in federal funds he had secured. The lab was used for after-school homework help, GED preparation, citizenship practice tests and job training.

According to NY1, sixteen people started the Centro Cívico in the 1970s as a meeting place for new immigrants. Its stated mission, in its nonprofit profile, is to "promote Colombian culture, values and traditions in the tri-state area."

Its profile lists classes in computers, English, GED preparation in Spanish, Spanish for children, guitar and folkloric dance, along with workshops and fairs on immigration, taxes, small business, health, art and culture. NY1 reported in 2019 that it still offered English, folklore dance and guitar lessons, with Amparo Gómez as president.
keyFacts: 1970s: Founded by sixteen people, per NY1.
Address on its profile: 9037 Corona Avenue, Elmhurst.
2010: $50,000 federal grant for a computer lab.
institutions.connectToWork: When a family needs both practical help and a place to belong, does your referral list show organizations that do both, or does it split them into separate categories?

institutions.name: Colombian American Service Association (C.A.S.A.)
body: In 1994, a group of Colombian Americans in Miami founded the Colombian American Service Association, known as C.A.S.A. According to its nonprofit profile, it advocates for and provides information and services to underserved Hispanic communities, promotes Hispanic heritage, and works to present a positive image of Colombia and its people. Its services include immigration help, legal and employment counseling, family support, housing and education. It reports helping more than 40,000 families since 1994.

A 2002 Florida House budget request shows how this worked in practice. C.A.S.A., then at 3138 Coral Way, sought $150,000 in state funds for its ICARE program (Immigrant Counseling Assistance Referral & Education), which offered case management, counseling, agency referrals and legal assistance, with a goal of serving about 1,750 families. The state had funded the program at $100,000 in fiscal year 1999–2000. The request was submitted by Juan Carlos Zapata.
GuideStar shows a Miami post office box and lists tax filings through 2025. The web address on that profile now leads to an unrelated immigration news site, so GuideStar is the safer place to start.
keyFacts: 1994: Founded by Colombian Americans in Miami.
Services: immigration, legal and employment counseling, family support, housing, education.
Fiscal year 1999–2000: State-funded ICARE program at $100,000.
Reports assisting more than 40,000 families since 1994.
institutions.connectToWork: If a state contract paid for a community-run program in your area, how would you know whether it met people's needs, and who would be left when the funding ended?

institutions.name: Little Colombia, Jackson Heights, Queens
institutions.location: Jackson Heights and Corona, Queens, New York City
body: Along Roosevelt Avenue in Queens, under the elevated tracks of the 7 train, the blocks from about 79th to 84th Streets are known as "Little Colombia."

According to NY1, Colombians have settled in Jackson Heights since the end of World War I, first mostly professionals and students. A recession in Colombia in the 1960s brought many more, and they spread into nearby Corona. One of the neighborhood's best-known figures is María Cano, the "Arepa Lady," a former judge in Medellín who moved to Jackson Heights with her four children in 1984 to escape the drug war and sold arepas from a cart under the 7 train. Her sons now run a shop on 37th Avenue.

A 2003 article in Harvard's ReVista described local activists organizing for peace and campaigning for Temporary Protected Status for Colombians. It reported that the 2000 Census counted 13,338 Colombians in Jackson Heights, and noted that the count may have missed many undocumented residents. NY1 reported in 2019 that many families had moved to the suburbs and Pennsylvania for cheaper housing. As of October 2026 the area is represented in the State Assembly by Colombian-born Catalina Cruz.
keyFacts: "Little Colombia": Roosevelt Avenue, roughly 79th to 84th Streets.
Settlement since the end of World War I, growing in the 1960s, per NY1.
1984: María Cano, the "Arepa Lady," arrived from Medellín.
2000 Census: 13,338 Colombians in Jackson Heights, as reported by ReVista, likely an undercount.
institutions.connectToWork: A person's support may still be in a neighborhood they left. How would your service learn where someone's people and help actually are, rather than where they live now?

sources.label: NY1, "How Jackson Heights earned the nickname Little Colombia" (2019)
ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America, "Colombian Immigration" (Spring 2003)

institutions.name: PACER Center
aliases: Parent Advocacy Coalition for Educational Rights
institutions.type: Parent center for families of children with disabilities
body: PACER Center (Parent Advocacy Coalition for Educational Rights) is a Minnesota parent center for families of children and young adults with disabilities. It is not specific to Colombians. It is listed here because parents in the 2022 Colombian study spoke about barriers to services and their authors called for culturally responsive parent education.

In July 2024 PACER announced a 16-month project funded by the Minnesota Department of Human Services, with Family Voices of Minnesota, for Latino and Somali families of children on the autism spectrum. It included parent support groups led by Latino and Somali staff in each language, training for parent volunteers, and tip sheets and videos in English, Spanish and Somali. The 16 months have since passed. Ask PACER what continues.
keyFacts: Announced July 17, 2024: 16-month Latino and Somali autism project.
Partner: Family Voices of Minnesota.
institutions.connectToWork: Before you refer a family to a program you heard about, how do you check that it is still running, and in which languages?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Colombian here covers people from the Andes, the Caribbean coast and the Pacific, Afro-Colombian and Indigenous people, and people who differ by generation, faith, education and immigration history. It also covers adoptees from Colombia raised in Minnesota, who may have little or no connection to what is below. We found no study of Colombian Minnesotans or Colombian Americans and disability, and none of Colombian adoptees in Minnesota. What follows comes from studies in Colombia and from one U.S. study of Latino parents in general, and each says which it is.
questions: How do you understand what is going on for you or your child? What words do you use for it at home?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or an assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who helps with care, and who would you like to be part of decisions?
Is your faith or church community a support for you? Would you like them involved?
What are your child's strengths, and what do you hope for their future?
Which language or languages do you prefer for meetings and written materials? If you use a sign language, which one?
If you were adopted from Colombia or grew up away from relatives there, what, if anything, would you like us to know about that?
Is there anything you want to know about who sees your information before we go further?
If you would like to tell me, did something in your life, such as an accident, an illness or a conflict, lead to this?

context.heading: What studies from Colombia have asked
body: A 2009 Colombian review (Castellanos Soriano and López) searched eight databases for articles from 1997 to early 2007 and selected 31 studies and literature reviews on disability and culture, not all from Colombia. It called the research "incipient," meaning just beginning. About 55 percent of the studies looked at how culture shapes the experience of families and caregivers. It says nothing about any one family.

A 2022 focus-group study with parents of autistic children in Colombia (Hughes, Magaña and colleagues) found four themes: how the diagnosis affected the family, systemic and societal barriers, the strengths parents saw in their child, and their hopes for the child's future. The abstract does not state how many parents took part. The authors recommended culturally responsive parent education.

sources.label: Castellanos Soriano and López, Avances en Enfermería 27(1), 2009
Hughes, Magaña, Gonzales, Núñez and Moreno-Angarita, Journal of Special Needs Education 25(1), 2022

context.heading: A U.S. study of Latino parents, not Colombians
body: In a study presented in 2015, 34 Latino parents of autistic children aged 2 to 22 (59 percent Mexican, 15 percent Puerto Rican, 24 percent other) were interviewed at home and asked whether a child's condition is a message from God. Most described their child as a positive sign, such as a blessing, part of God's plan, or a test. Five saw the child as a punishment. Others pointed to nature, and some said the wider culture sees punishment but that they rejected that view. About half the families attended religious services at least a few times a year. It is a small sample and a conference abstract, and no Colombian result can be drawn from it. Ask, and do not assume either a faith or a medical explanation.

sources.label: Salkas, Marques and Magaña, International Meeting for Autism Research (2015), abstract

context.heading: Conflict, stigma and the gap between law and experience
body: A 2025 preprint from Colombia, not yet peer-reviewed (González Ballesteros and colleagues), looked back over qualitative research on psychosocial disability. It reported a consistent gap between legal protections and lived experience, especially for Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities affected by violence, and said that people with disabilities had limited part in processes such as peacebuilding. It describes Colombia, not people who have since moved. Some people who came from Colombia lived through conflict or displacement and others did not, so it is for the person to tell you, if they wish.

sources.label: González Ballesteros and colleagues, SciELO Preprints (August 2025)

context.heading: Language and sign language
body: Rights documents in Spanish use "persona con discapacidad" (person with a disability), as Human Rights Watch does. Mariana Lozano describes herself as a woman with an intellectual disability. Ask each person which words they use.

Colombia's national institute for Deaf people, INSOR, works in Colombian Sign Language (Lengua de Señas Colombiana), recognized in Colombian law since 1996, and keeps a national registry of its interpreters. It is a different language from ASL, so ask rather than assume. Arrange qualified interpreting through the appropriate language-access or disability-access process; do not assume a child or relative can serve as an interpreter. Do not assume that someone from Colombia reads or speaks Spanish. An adoptee raised in Minnesota may speak only English.

sources.label: Instituto Nacional para Sordos (INSOR)
Human Rights Watch, "Colombian Disability Rights Activist Honored" (December 4, 2023)

context.heading: Fear of systems, and what we could not find
body: We found no study of Colombian families in the U.S. on fear of public systems. Immigration status may matter to any family, and it may not. Say only what your agency's current written policy supports about who sees a person's information, and do not make promises beyond it.

We also found no Colombian research on traditional healing and disability services, and no source on who in a Colombian family makes care decisions. Ask each family. Minnesota has no Colombian disability organization that we could find, and we could not find a Colombian American disability advocate with a public record. MPR News reports that Colombia Live's dancers include adoptees, and that families call it a second family, which is the closest thing to a Minnesota connection in this material.

sources.label: MPR News, Colombia Live (December 21, 2023)

organizations.intro: We found no active Colombian civic association in Minnesota. Colombian life in the Twin Cities shows up most clearly through Colombia Live, through the Chicago consulate's civil-society session held in Minneapolis in November 2024, and through Latino organizations and media that are not specific to Colombians. Two Minnesota groups were not listed because we found nothing recent: Integración Cultural Colombiana en Minnesota, whose newest dated post is from January 2019, and the Asociación de Colombianos en Minnesota, whose website no longer loads. MPR News reported in 2012 on La Semana, a weeklong camp in Lakeville for children adopted from Latin America, with about 500 campers that year. We found nothing newer on it. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.location: St. Paul, 540 Fairview Avenue North, Suite 200

entries.purpose: A south Minneapolis parish with Spanish and English Masses, listed through October 2026, and a Spanish-language parish office. Not specific to Colombians. We found no parish in Minnesota with a Colombian ministry.

entries.purpose: A daily news site for Latino Minnesotans, with stories dated October 2026.

entries.purpose: A Spanish-language paper from St. Paul Publishing, delivered to Hispanic centers in the Twin Cities. The publisher's site lists a November 2026 issue.

entries.name: Consulate General of Colombia in Chicago
entries.purpose: The consular office for Minnesota and nearby states. It may be where a person gets identity or civil records from Colombia. It ran a civil-society session on migration in Minneapolis on November 9, 2024.

entries.name: Colombia Nos Une
entries.purpose: The Colombian Foreign Ministry's program for Colombians abroad. It convenes civil-society discussions on migration, including the 2024 Minneapolis session.

entries.name: Colombian-American Association of Florida (ASOCOL Tampa)
entries.purpose: A small volunteer group serving the Tampa Bay area. Its site lists scholarships for 2026–2027, and its GuideStar profile lists free help with taxes, immigration forms and translations, and holiday food baskets. Serves Florida only.

entries.name: Colombian American Association
entries.location: United States; its social media name points to New York
entries.purpose: A two-country chamber of commerce that describes itself as connecting Colombia and the U.S. and runs an incubation program for Colombian entrepreneurs. A business network, not a service agency.

entries.name: Colombian-American Chamber of Commerce (AmCham Colombia)
entries.location: Bogotá, with offices in other Colombian cities
entries.purpose: A nonprofit based in Colombia that promotes U.S.–Colombia trade and investment. It is not a group of Colombians in the United States.

entries.name: El Tiempo
entries.purpose: A national daily founded in 1911.

entries.name: El Espectador
entries.purpose: A national newspaper founded in Medellín in 1887. National news, politics and investigative reporting.

entries.name: El Colombiano
entries.purpose: A regional daily covering Medellín, Antioquia, Colombia and the world.

entries.purpose: A private Colombian television network with telenovelas, entertainment and news. We could not confirm its U.S. carriage.

entries.name: RCN Televisión / Nuestra Tele
